source.title: Evaluating Tiny Recursive Models Across Training for Code Generation
source.authors: Anjani Sirivella; Aanisha Newaz; Glaucia Melo

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares architectures at matched parameter count and reports held-out fit, bearing on whether architectural differences have little effect on loss. It does not fit scaling laws or test compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no power-law fits, parameter/token/compute scaling sweep, or compute-optimal allocation. Its training-trajectory findings concern checkpoint-dependent rankings, not scaling-law exponents. The rows below are limited to the matched-parameter architecture comparison and its reported fit metrics.
record.test_reason: The study fits no scaling law and runs no parameter, token or compute sweep. Its only matched-parameter contrast is a weight-shared recursive model trained with deep supervision against a plain 2-layer transformer. That is not a depth/width/shape change of a standard transformer at fixed N, which is what V4 names. The recursive arm runs a 20-layer computation per token (about 175× per-step time) and uses a different training objective (mean loss over 3 supervision steps). So the loss gap reflects extra compute per parameter and objective changes, not shape. Training is also 40 epochs on a small repeated corpus with completion-only loss, not held-out pretraining loss in the Kaplan/Hoffmann sense. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as background and for counting non-embedding parameters.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct but incomplete. The authors also conclude that at equal effective depth the 20-layer transformer fits and generates better at its validation optimum (val loss 1.154). TRM-AR's remaining edge there is resistance to overfitting, not capability. Its efficiency is in parameters, not compute. Single-checkpoint rankings mislead (the fit ranking reverses twice), so recursive models should be evaluated on fit and generation across the training trajectory.
record.recipe_differences: This is an architecture and training-trajectory comparison, not a power-law scaling experiment or a fit of compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The fit ranking against the iso-depth model changes across training checkpoints; validation-based checkpoint selection resolves the trajectory differently from reading an arbitrary epoch. This is checkpoint sensitivity, not sensitivity of scaling-law fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched total parameters (~27.8M; ~2.1M non-embedding), a weight-shared recursive model looping a 2-layer block to effective depth 20, trained with deep supervision, reaches lower validation loss than a plain 2-layer transformer (1.277 vs 1.379). It recovers ~45% of the gap to a 20-layer model with ~10× the non-embedding parameters, at ~175× the per-step time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed parameter count, adding compute per parameter via weight-shared recursion lowers loss, recovering part of the gap to a model with more unique parameters, so parameter count alone does not determine loss when per-token compute is decoupled from N.

record.problems: Only three seeds per arm; the study reports no significance tests. The matched-parameter comparison confounds recursion with deep supervision. The corpus is synthetic and templated, the evidence covers a narrow model and task setting, and the parameter-lean arms' validation optima are right-censored at the 40-epoch budget.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for scaling-law versions: the paper does not report power-law fits or a scaling sweep. Training-trajectory and generation results do not measure V4's loss comparison beyond the matched-parameter fit metrics retained above.

untested.parts: No loss-vs-parameters, tokens or compute sweep or power-law fit.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No depth/width/aspect-ratio variation of standard transformers at fixed non-embedding parameter count. The recursive comparison changes compute per token and the objective.
Repeated-data multi-epoch training is used but no scaling form is fitted. No other modalities and no fine-tuning or transfer laws.
Judge scores are reported for three arms only, not as a function of scale or loss trend.
Checkpoint-dependent rankings are shown, but nothing on fitted exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'challenges' label is dropped: the contrast is not a shape change at fixed N but a change in compute per token and in training objective, which Kaplan's shape result does not cover. Other caveats: three seeds, right-censored optima for the two parameter-lean arms, a synthetic corpus, and repeated-data training. The vanilla-2L vs vanilla-20L contrast differs in parameters, so it is not a V4 test either.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss trends in parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and how either varies with compute.

The study tests one parameter-matched architecture comparison on synthetic code data. It does not vary width or test a broad range of depth, architecture, model scales, or datasets; the recursive model also uses deep supervision, which is not disentangled from recursion.
Other modalities, repeated-data comparisons as a scaling-law test, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
Predictability of downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices or setup, and departures from a single power law.

reader_labels.condition: The tested matched-parameter comparison on the TINY-CODES Python task, at validation-selected checkpoints
reader_labels.reason: The recursive configuration has lower validation loss and test perplexity than the parameter-matched plain transformer, rather than showing no meaningful architecture-associated difference; the comparison is confounded by deep supervision (r1–r4).
